title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 57–58
description: Future technologies, environmental projections, genetic terminology, changing societies, fossil fuels, renewable energy and efficient consumption.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied Advanced third-edition textbook for personal language study. The vocabulary targets and usage patterns follow the relevant units and exercises; all Portuguese translations, English explanations and example sentences are independently authored. The textbook passages, exercises and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching sections, technology and energy tables, usage notes, exercises 57.1–57.5 and 58.1–58.3, and Unit 57–58 answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Conservative broad British IPA for individual words whose transcriptions can be supplied with confidence; complex phrases have blank IPA rather than conjectural connected-speech transcriptions.
audit.languagePolicy: All descriptions, titles, examples, notes and other learner-facing fields are English-only except for natural Brazilian Portuguese in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Checked source pages, tables, numbered explanations, exercise tasks and corresponding answer-key entries; independently authored the examples and notes; checked meanings, provenance and registers. Performed static JSON-schema, ID, required-field, audio-target and text-quality validation against the same-edition canonical reference. No browser, speech-recognition or app-import test was run.
audit.limitations: No MP3 recordings are bundled. Browser TTS, speech recognition and VocabLab import require runtime verification. Future predictions and medical or environmental claims are language-learning examples, not forecasts or technical advice.

units.title: Unit 57 — Technology of the future
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 57. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Discuss emerging technologies, smart environments, interplanetary travel and the scope of nanotechnology.
Distinguish future projections, environmental risks and genetic concepts using precise advanced collocations.
Use foresee, envisage, destiny and doomsday scenario with their appropriate implications and register.
Describe globalisation, the global village, families and inequality without treating predictions as established facts.

sectionsChecked: A, B and C teaching sections, the technology table, definitions and sociological examples

items.example: The research campus plans to introduce smart buildings that adjust lighting and ventilation automatically.
items.note: Buildings with electronically controlled systems; smart describes systems using digital information to respond to conditions.

items.example: Smart homes can coordinate heating, security and lighting through connected devices.
items.note: The home-focused version of a computer-controlled building; do not assume every smart home is entirely autonomous.

items.pt: carro inteligente; veículo com sistemas digitais integrados
items.example: The prototype smart car detects obstacles and warns the driver before a collision.
items.note: Smart indicates computer-based functionality, not necessarily full autonomous driving.

items.example: Engineers are studying propulsion systems that might make interplanetary travel more practical.
items.note: Travel between planets, rather than travel merely around Earth.

items.example: Commercial companies hope to make space tourism accessible beyond a small group of wealthy travellers.
items.note: Travel into space for leisure rather than scientific research; currently a specialised activity.

items.example: Nanotechnology enables researchers to manipulate materials at extremely small scales.
items.note: Science and technology involving control of matter at roughly atomic or molecular scales.

items.pt: cirurgia minimamente invasiva; cirurgia por pequenos orifícios
items.example: The surgeon recommended keyhole surgery because it might require a smaller incision.
items.note: British term for surgery performed through small openings; also called minimally invasive surgery in many contexts.

items.pt: cenário catastrófico; previsão do pior desfecho
items.example: The report outlines a doomsday scenario in which prolonged drought disrupts food supplies.
items.note: An extremely pessimistic prediction, not an inevitable outcome.

items.pt: destino; futuro que se acredita estar reservado
items.example: The novelist imagines a society in which technology determines humanity's destiny.
items.note: What is believed to happen in the future; often carries a suggestion of inevitability.

items.pt: sufocado pela poluição; tomado pela poluição
items.example: Without stricter controls, the valley could become choked with pollution from factories.
items.note: Choked with means so filled with something harmful that normal functioning becomes difficult; figurative here.

items.example: Several native species could become extinct if their habitats continue to shrink.
items.note: Extinct describes a species no longer surviving anywhere, not merely endangered.

items.example: Analysts foresee severe water shortages unless consumption patterns change.
items.note: Predict a likely future development; often implies a reasoned expectation.

items.pt: megacidade; cidade com mais de dez milhões de habitantes
items.example: The planners studied how a mega-city could maintain reliable public transport.
items.note: In this source, a city whose population exceeds ten million.

items.example: Gridlocked traffic delayed emergency vehicles across the city centre.
items.note: A situation in which traffic cannot move; stronger than ordinary congestion.

items.example: After the crash, the ring road remained gridlocked for hours.
items.note: Often predicative; can describe a road or city in which vehicles cannot move.

items.example: A rapid population explosion put additional pressure on housing and water supplies.
items.note: A very rapid increase in population, not simply a high population.

items.example: Crop failures could lead to widespread food shortages in the region.
items.note: A shortage is an insufficient supply relative to demand; usually plural in this collocation.

items.example: Water shortages have prompted the city to reconsider its long-term supply plans.
items.note: A lack of adequate water supply; distinct from water pollution.

items.example: The committee discussed whether genetic modification could improve the crops' resilience.
items.note: Changing an organism's genetic material; the expression does not itself indicate whether a change is beneficial.

items.example: Genetic engineering has created new opportunities for developing disease-resistant crops.
items.note: The deliberate manipulation of genetic material; closely related to genetic modification.

items.pt: culturas geneticamente modificadas; plantas transgênicas (conforme o caso)
items.example: The farm trial compared genetically modified crops with conventional varieties.
items.note: GM is pronounced as two letters; genetically modified need not always mean transgenic.

items.example: The debate centred on how genetically modified food should be labelled.
items.note: GM food refers to food produced using genetically modified organisms or ingredients.

items.example: The article examines the potential of gene therapy for certain inherited disorders.
items.note: A medical approach that introduces or changes genetic material; applications and outcomes vary by condition.

items.example: Researchers hope that improved treatments will eventually eradicate the disease.
items.note: To remove a problem or disease completely; stronger than reduce.

items.example: Mapping the human genome has contributed to research on inherited conditions.
items.note: The complete genetic information of a human being, not merely one gene.

items.example: The designers envisage a future in which most appliances share information automatically.
items.note: Form a mental picture of a possible future; unlike foresee, does not necessarily mean predict it will happen.

items.example: The ethics seminar discussed the controversial idea of a designer baby.
items.note: A socially and ethically charged term for a baby whose characteristics are deliberately selected or altered.

items.example: The documentary explored the ethical questions raised by the cloning of animals.
items.note: Producing a genetically identical copy; the word also has wider non-biological uses.

items.word: breakdown of the traditional family structure
items.example: The study considers whether migration contributes to the breakdown of the traditional family structure.
items.note: Breakdown suggests weakening or disruption; the statement represents a social interpretation, not a universal fact.

items.pt: família nuclear; núcleo familiar de pais e filhos
items.example: The survey distinguished the nuclear family from larger multigenerational households.
items.note: Traditionally a parent or parents and their children; the textbook illustrates a conventional father-mother model.

items.example: Globalisation has changed where companies manufacture products and recruit employees.
items.note: Growing economic and social interconnectedness across national borders; British spelling.

items.example: Instant communication makes the world feel like a global village.
items.note: Metaphor for the world operating as an interconnected community.

items.example: The science-fiction novel depicts first contact with extraterrestrial beings.
items.note: Beings originating beyond Earth; use as a concept in speculative discussion, not evidence of their existence.

items.word: the gulf between rich and poor
items.pt: o abismo entre ricos e pobres
items.example: Campaigners fear that unequal access to education may widen the gulf between rich and poor.
items.note: Gulf metaphorically means a large difference or division; collocates with widen, narrow and bridge.

items.pt: aumentar o abismo; aprofundar a desigualdade
items.example: Unequal internet access could widen the gulf between prosperous and disadvantaged communities.
items.note: Widen means make an existing difference greater; opposite narrow the gulf.

items.example: The council may need to take drastic measures to prevent further water contamination.
items.note: Drastic measures are severe or far-reaching actions, not minor adjustments.

units.title: Unit 58 — Energy: from fossil fuels to windmills
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 58. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Identify fossil-fuel infrastructure and distinguish offshore from onshore facilities.
Describe the principal renewable and other energy-generation technologies using accurate collocations.
Use energy consumption, power-hungry, energy-efficient and carbon footprint naturally.
Discuss finite resources, energy-saving behaviour and environmental impact precisely.

sectionsChecked: A, B and C teaching sections, labelled energy sources, numbered definitions and Common mistakes box
Exercises 58.1–58.3, including pictures and the answer key

items.example: The island aims to reduce its dependence on fossil fuels over the next decade.
items.note: Coal, oil and gas formed from ancient organic material; non-renewable on human timescales.

items.example: The new oil well is expected to begin production after safety checks.
items.note: A hole drilled into the ground to extract oil; a well need not be offshore.

items.pt: em alto-mar; situado afastado da costa
items.example: The company plans an offshore survey before approving the drilling site.
items.note: Away from the coast or at sea; contrast with onshore.

items.example: Safety inspectors visited the offshore drilling platform before operations resumed.
items.note: Structure at sea used to drill for oil or gas; distinguishes a drilling platform from a refinery.

items.example: The region plans to replace an ageing coal-fired power station with lower-emission generation.
items.note: Coal-fired specifies that coal supplies the energy used for generation.

items.example: The abandoned coal mine was converted into a local heritage site.
items.note: A site from which coal is extracted, often through underground workings.

items.example: A new gas pipeline will connect the processing plant with coastal customers.
items.note: A long pipe for transporting gas; a pipeline may also carry oil or other fluids.

items.pt: duto; tubulação de transporte de longa distância
items.example: Engineers inspected the pipeline for signs of corrosion.
items.note: Used to move liquid or gas over long distances; also a metaphor for planned work.

items.example: The regional authority is investing in renewable energy to diversify electricity production.
items.note: Energy replenished naturally on a human timescale; unlike finite fossil-fuel deposits.

items.pt: fontes renováveis de energia; energias renováveis
items.example: The utility intends to expand renewables while modernising its grid.
items.note: Countable plural noun for renewable energy sources or technologies.

items.pt: em terra; localizado em terra firme
items.example: The developer selected an onshore site for the wind farm rather than an offshore location.
items.note: Opposite of offshore; refers to location on land, including energy installations.

items.example: An onshore wind farm was proposed near the agricultural area.
items.note: A group of wind turbines situated on land rather than at sea.

items.example: The wind farm supplies electricity to several nearby towns.
items.note: A collection of wind turbines generating electricity at one site.

items.example: Each wind turbine sends operating data to the maintenance centre.
items.note: A machine that converts energy from the wind into mechanical rotation and then electricity.

items.example: The school installed solar panels on the roof to generate electricity.
items.note: In this unit, devices that convert sunlight into electrical energy.

items.example: The hydroelectric power station uses flowing water to drive its turbines.
items.note: Generates electricity from moving or falling water; the book uses hydroelectric.

items.example: Agricultural residues can provide biomass for certain energy systems.
items.note: Organic material from plants or animals used as fuel or an energy resource.

items.example: Researchers are assessing the potential for tidal power in the estuary.
items.note: Electricity generated using the periodic movement of sea tides; differs from wave power.

items.example: Wave power remains an option for the exposed coastline.
items.note: Energy harnessed from surface waves rather than the tide.

items.example: The government approved a feasibility study for a nuclear power station.
items.note: Generates electricity using nuclear reactions; the book mentions it among energy options, not as a fossil fuel.

items.example: Nuclear energy is debated alongside other low-carbon electricity sources.
items.note: Energy released through nuclear processes; it is not ordinarily classified as renewable.

items.example: Geothermal energy can provide reliable heating in regions with suitable geology.
items.note: Heat from inside the Earth used for heating or electricity generation.

items.example: Solar energy offers opportunities for electricity production in sunny regions.
items.note: Energy obtained from the sun; a wider term than electricity from solar panels alone.

items.example: The laboratory tracked energy consumption before and after upgrading its equipment.
items.note: The quantity of energy used; consumption is the noun corresponding to consume.

items.pt: que consome muita energia; de alto consumo elétrico
items.example: The old server was power-hungry and required extensive cooling.
items.note: Describes equipment that uses unusually large amounts of energy; often before a noun.

items.example: Modern appliances often display an energy-efficiency rating to help shoppers compare models.
items.note: Typically household devices such as refrigerators and washing machines; plural of appliance.

items.example: The facilities team will monitor energy use throughout the winter.
items.note: Monitor means check or measure repeatedly over time, not merely observe once.

items.example: Heating systems consume energy even when operating at reduced capacity.
items.note: Consume is a transitive verb meaning use up a resource.

items.pt: em modo de espera; em stand-by
items.example: Several devices were left on standby overnight and continued drawing power.
items.note: Operating in a low-power waiting state, not necessarily completely switched off.

items.pt: carro que bebe muito combustível; veículo de alto consumo
items.example: The large vehicle was criticised as a gas-guzzler despite its comfortable interior.
items.note: Informal and often disapproving label for a vehicle that uses a lot of fuel.

items.pt: energeticamente eficiente; de baixo consumo de energia
items.example: The new heat pump is more energy-efficient than the older model.
items.note: Uses relatively little energy to provide the same or similar service; hyphenated before a noun.

items.example: Improving energy efficiency reduced operating costs without changing the factory's output.
items.note: How effectively energy is converted into useful services; not merely consuming less by reducing activity.

items.pt: distância percorrida pelos alimentos desde a origem até o consumidor
items.example: The campaign encouraged shoppers to consider food miles alongside production methods.
items.note: Distance travelled by food before sale; it alone does not measure total environmental impact.

items.example: The engineer compared fuel consumption across several operating conditions.
items.note: The amount of fuel used; often reported per distance or unit of work.

items.example: The university estimated its carbon footprint from travel, heating and electricity.
items.note: Measure of greenhouse-gas emissions associated with activities; the book explains it in terms of carbon dioxide.

items.example: Replacing short flights with rail journeys may help reduce your carbon footprint.
items.note: Common collocation used for lowering emissions associated with personal activities.

items.example: The department introduced remote meetings to cut out unnecessary journeys.
items.note: Cut out means stop or remove something entirely, not merely reduce its frequency.

items.example: Oil supplies are finite, so long-term planning cannot assume unlimited availability.
items.note: Describes something with a limit or an end; opposite infinite.

items.pt: jazidas de combustível; reservas naturais de combustíveis
items.example: The geological survey identified fuel deposits beneath the valley.
items.note: Natural underground accumulations of energy resources; the book refers to coal, oil and gas deposits.

items.example: The community fears that its local gas reserves may eventually run out.
items.note: Intransitive phrasal verb meaning be used up; a resource runs out without a direct object.
